speaker: The Chairman
text: Head I, Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF).

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Chairman, I move, "That the total sum allocated to Head I of the Estimates be reduced by $100." Members on both sides of the House have spoken passionately in this House about social mobility in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, there is no monopoly on compassion for the least amongst us and no monopoly on ideas to uplift them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Social mobility is one centre of gravity in MSF's work.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, as Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chair, I thought to use this speech to contribute to the conversation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And here, I would like to declare that I am also working in a foundation focussed on social mobility.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But first, let us frame the challenge of social mobility in Singapore precisely.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Singapore has uplifted lower-income households significantly over the decades.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In technical terms, Singapore has kept absolute social mobility very much alive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Each generation has, on the whole, including those in the lowest-income segment, been able to achieve much better life outcomes than the previous generation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Yet, between households, higher-income households are accumulating advantages even more quickly than lower-income household.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Therefore, within each generation, the starting points in life between children from higher- and lower-income families are moving further apart, and the opportunities gap throughout life between children from higher- and lower-income families is widening, resulting in larger inequalities in outcomes much later in life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In technical terms, therefore, relative social mobility in Singapore is slowing even as we have kept absolute mobility very much alive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The Ministry of Finance's (MOF's) Occasional Papers, in both 2015 and 2025, bear this out.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The key measure for relative mobility is the income distribution of children, in their 30s, born to fathers who were in the bottom 20% of earners, in their 40s.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In other words, the starting condition for these children was, being born into the bottom 20% by income, and the measure is where these children ended up by income in their adult lives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In an ideal world, 20% of these children would themselves end up in the top 20% of earners in their cohorts; 20% will end up being in the bottom 20% of earners – like their fathers, and so on.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, relative social mobility in Singapore has been slowing even as we sustained broad-based progress for all.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And the natural tendency will be for relative mobility to continue slowing, as it has in many other advanced economies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I must point out, though, that we have been doing better than other advanced economies in relative mobility.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, we are not doing badly at all.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But Singapore has never been one to define our values and ideals solely on how we outperform other societies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We chart our own path and we set our own values and ideals.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I think we must continue to be a society where relative mobility is alive as much as possible and indeed, strengthened if at all possible.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Keep the measure as close to 20% as possible, and lean against the natural pressures of slowing relative mobility with time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In concrete terms, this means pushing against the natural pressures of ever further starting points in life and the pressures of an ever-widening opportunities gap that compounds through life for our children of today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Our families at the bottom are not stuck – far from it – but we must help their children keep up with families at the top who are pulling away faster.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Help children at the bottom keep up from the start of their lives, and through life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Or as Ms Sylvia Lim said in this House back in 2018, children impacted by their parents' circumstances must be "supported or facilitated to break out".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: However, while we can look to the Government, with its policy levers, to secure broad-based progress for all, in other words, to deliver absolute mobility, it is quite a different story for relative mobility.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Keeping relative social mobility alive, essentially, containing that opportunities gap between your children and mine, almost by definition, cannot be left to the Government, or for that matter, the social sector, alone.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Those who have done well and can provide the most to their children must play an active role and become part of the solution, to create opportunities for those children who start off with less.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Indeed, well-known researchers, like Raj Chetty and Matt Jackson, are showing that in America at least.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And indeed, as Teo You Yenn puts it in her book, "This is What Inequality Looks Like", inequality, in opportunities, through life, is not just the result of policies, but also how everyone, at the top and bottom and in between interact and choose to interact with these policies, interact with one another within a social context and do and do not do certain things.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, those who have done well must play an active role to create opportunities for those children who start off with much less.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This is what a "we first" and mobile society in Singapore can look like.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And I think becoming such a society and keeping relative mobility alive in this way, will be a defining challenge of our times.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, what do we need to get there?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: First, I think we need scientific knowledge and understanding.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, in the same speech in 2018, called for longitudinal studies that will, "track the fate of families (at the bottom) over time" and indeed, go "beyond numbers to dig deep into the daily lives and evaluate the reasons why they do not seem to be able to catch up with the rest of society." MOF's Occasional Papers in 2015 and 2025 do provide a longitudinal view on how families at the bottom are doing.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But I agree with Ms Lim and today, I want to build on her call.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In very technical and academic terms, we can use theoretical networking games and micro-founded structural approaches that overcome the reflection problem arising in reduced-form peer effects analysis in econometrics to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But in simple terms, we should be aiming for models that show how individuals make decisions and assume certain trajectories in life based on intrinsic factors, extrinsic factors and the influence of peers on one another.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And all this is possible only if we have the right dataset.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, we must start with data, the right type of data, collected to the right fidelity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We need data on the social networks of Singaporeans at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We need data on cognitive and behavioural traits, on their participation in the economy, not only in the formal sector, but also, and perhaps especially, in the informal sector.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We need data on participation in credit facilities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Again, both formal and informal and we will need such data over a long period of time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: To my knowledge, there is no such dataset in Singapore perhaps precisely because it is very challenging to collect such data, to high fidelity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It requires extensive and deep fieldwork, over a long period of time and first, building strong relationships of trust.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It requires adherence to high ethical standards, including privacy standards, that will do no harm to the vulnerable that we are seeking to understand and ultimately uplift.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And all these mean it will require considerable and sustained funding.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And by the way, such a dataset goes well beyond administrative data.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But even with such research, by definition, we will only truly know the outcomes of what we do today 35 to 40 years later.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Social mobility is that longitudinal by its very nature.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Put another way, we cannot wait for longitudinal research to conclude, to tell us what we should we do now, to close the opportunities gap for our children of today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Deciding what to do now to close that opportunities gap will thus be as much art as it is science.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We will need to look to whatever evidence base is available and apply judgement, consider ideas thoroughly, try to do no harm if at all possible, but act now.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And then, in 35 to 40 years down the road, we will truly find out how we have done.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But so, what do we need to do now, systemically, to close the opportunities gap from the start of life and through life?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Instead, we need a system of interlocking solutions, across multiple domains – academic, non-academic, social capital formation, financial stability, housing, health – each solution working alongside the others, to collectively close the opportunities gap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The harder work – the hardest work – is often in scaling and sustaining at scale.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Early life matters and we must intervene heavily in the early years, but we cannot stop there.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And the Government can play a leadership role here to signpost, coordinate, support, resource and galvanise.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Section 12(1)(b) requires personal welfare donees be individuals.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Organisations are allowed only for property and affairs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Office of Public Guardian's (OPG's) own list of registered professional deputies illustrates the consequence.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Six social workers and one accountant from TOUCH Community Services are listed individually: same address at Bukit Merah Central, same email, same phone number.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They function as an organisation, but the law forces the appointment to be personal.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When that social worker leaves, the donor must pay to appoint a replacement.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In deputyship cases, the cost comes from the incapacitated person's own assets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It seems wrong to make the donor pay for a gap in the law.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is also a practical issue with personal appointments.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: LPAs are made years or decades before activation, meaning individual donees may have retired, emigrated or died.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is considerable uncertainty whether donees appointed years ago can take up the appointment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Australia's states have addressed this through Public Guardian offices, providing continuity for personal welfare decisions, regardless of staff changes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Beyond that, could Singapore's Public Guardian serve as donee of last resort, as Australian states have done?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will OPG also issue guidance on what happens when a professional donee falls off the register?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And will OPG consider prescribed fee guidelines for professional donee services, given this is a fiduciary service for the most vulnerable and not a competitive market?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Momentum has built up as the benefits of making LPAs become more widely understood.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My purpose today is to highlight two groups of people who may not be benefiting from the LPA regime for different reasons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They are first, those without any relative or friend to appoint; and secondly, our low-wage foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, those without any relative or friend to appoint.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such an option will assist those donors as the appointment will withstand the passage of time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second group who currently have difficulties with LPAs are foreign workers in Singapore under work permits.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though they are relatively young, some of them work under conditions where the risk of serious injury, including mental incapacity, is ever present.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Examples include those in physically demanding industries, such as the construction and marine sectors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These migrant workers do not have next-of-kin in Singapore and their friends may not be conversant with navigating Singapore's systems and services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Should they suddenly lose mental capacity, they would benefit if a donee could assist them to make decisions about their personal welfare or manage their funds, for example, to send money back to their loved ones at home.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These include volunteers who care deeply about migrant worker welfare and wish to contribute.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are also lawyers who are willing to issue LPAs without charge or take on the role of a volunteer donee if needed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the issue the workers face is the high cost of registration of LPAs for foreigners.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For our low-wage migrant workers, this fee is prohibitive, accounting for a significant portion of their monthly salary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The public guardian should not have a blanket registration fee for all foreigners, which applies to our high-wage Employment Pass (EP) holders and low-wage foreign work permit holders alike.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our low-wage foreign workers work under tough physical conditions, and we rely on them to do much of the work that Singaporeans are not inclined to do.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a gesture would go a long way to showing that we really care.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, MSF has consistently emphasised the importance of strong families and I support that objective.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: However, when we speak about "strong families", we must ask: what families are we speaking about and are our policies fully aligned with the lived realities of Singaporean households today?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Unlike dual-income households, single parents must shoulder both breadwinning and caregiving responsibilities without internal household support.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: While MSF provides assistance schemes, much of the framework remains largely designed around a dual-family baseline.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: These are parents who work full-time, care for their children alone and yet live one unexpected bill away from financial instability.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Does MSF track long-term economic mobility outcomes specifically for single-parent households?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Are there plans to recalibrate housing, childcare and work-support schemes to better reflect the time and income constraints unique to single parents?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Has the Ministry conducted a comprehensive review of whether current family policies inadvertently assume a nuclear, dual-parent model?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, this leads to a broader question.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Much of MSF's effort to encourage strong families appears centred on public education campaigns promoting marriage, parenting and shared norms.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: While public messaging has its place, many families today are not struggling because of a lack of awareness.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: They are struggling because of cumulative pressures – cost of living, housing affordability, expensive childcare, enrichment expectations and long working hours.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: At the national level, we rightly prioritise workforce development and economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But do our family policies receive the same systemic priority?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Or have we unintentionally reduced family stability to a messaging exercise rather than treating it as an economic and cross-ministerial design issue?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Is the traditional nuclear family still the dominant policy reference point?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, this policy cut is not intended to diminish support for families.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Rather, it signals the need to reassess whether our frameworks have kept pace with social change.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: If we are serious about building strong families, then our policies must be designed not around idealised models but around the realities Singaporean households actually live with today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, families in Singapore face considerable pressures in our fast-paced and competitive society.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many must manage the cost of housing, education, healthcare and daily living.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For lower-income households, these demands can be especially heavy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At the same time, long working hours in pursuit of job security and career progression often reduce the time parents spend with their children, placing strain on family relationships.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Strong and resilient families, therefore, require sustained support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Strengthening Families programme plays an important role through counselling, parenting workshops and family bonding activities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As family needs grow more complex, how does MSF intend to further enhance and scale up the programme to better support families facing multiple stresses?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, I would also like to raise a related issue.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Overseas research has observed inter-generational patterns of children being born out of wedlock, often influenced by socio-economic factors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should be mindful to prevent such cycles from taking root in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While upholding the importance of marriage and stable families, we must also ensure that children are not disadvantaged by their circumstances of birth.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MSF review how we can better support unwed parents in meeting their children's needs and whether more local research can be conducted to better understand and prevent potential inter-generational cycles?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) awarded her centre's Make*Believe programme the Innovation Award in 2023.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The National Institute of Early Childhood Development (NIEC) featured her as the expert voice on play-based learning.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: When Government subsidy prices 80% of the market at $610 to $650, that becomes what preschools should cost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Parents are not choosing Anchor Operator (AOP) pedagogy over play-based learning.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: At a $1,000 differential, there is no real choice.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: AOP and POP salary targets funded by subsidy becomes a sector-wide wage benchmark.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Independents must match or lose teachers, not to better pedagogy but to better subsidised pay.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Every time salary targets rise, independents' costs rise with them, but revenue does not.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The 20% is expected to innovate, but with what?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: From 2024 to 2026, only AOPs and POPs had subsidised talent development.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Independents competed for the same shrinking pool of educators at full cost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: This is the same regulator funding one team's player development budget and asking the other why they cannot keep up.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The end state – two tiers and nothing in between.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Mass market, Government preschools on one side; ultra-premium international schools on the other.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The mid-tier, wherein Montessori, Reggio, play-based and inclusive programmes for children with diverse needs actually live, is collapsing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Progress is when what was once a boutique pedagogy becomes the base we build for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: In December 2025, its government revamped the national preschool curriculum to prioritise play-based, child-centred learning.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: In April, Kuala Lumpur hosts the World Forum on Early Care and Education, with 500 participants from over 40 countries.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Malaysian educators invite Singaporean operators to speak at their forums on play- and project-based learning.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Our neighbours are investing in what our funding model makes unviable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: If they are right about early childhood, and I believe they are, a pedagogy gap will open across the Causeway, as we drive out the very educators they want to learn from.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: If the subsidy follows a child to any licensed, quality-assured centre, parents, all parents, can choose the pedagogy the Government's own agencies say works.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: When the gap is $80, parents can weigh the differences.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: If a teacher is L2 certified, why should their salary support depend on which operator employs them?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: What is missing is a funding structure that lets parents act on the agreement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, accessible, affordable and quality preschools are fundamental to giving every child a strong start in life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: First, accessibility means ensuring that preschool places are available and conveniently located across our neighbourhoods, so families can enrol their children without undue difficulty.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Second, affordability ensures that families from all income levels can assess early childhood education without financial strain.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: A nurturing and stimulating environment supported by well-trained educators, age-appropriate curricula and safe facilities enables children's holistic development.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: A strong core of early childhood educators lays the foundation for our children's cognitive, social, emotional and physical growth, preparing them well for primary school and beyond.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: At the same time, our early childhood educators are taking on increasing responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: With smaller families and rising parental expectations, educators are expected to do more than ever before.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: This is further compounded by manpower challenges and the time required to fill vacancies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In this regard, can MSF consider expanding the roles and capabilities of learning support educators beyond special needs support, so that they can help augment and relieve pressures on our stretched early childhood workforce.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Often at the same time and often with the same leave pool.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my maiden speech, I said that caregiving is work and we can and should do more to support our caregivers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, childcare and extended childcare leave remains the only legislated form of ongoing paid caregiving leave.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each parent receives two to six days a year, regardless of how many children they have.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet we know that caregiving demands multiply with each child and does not divide neatly between siblings.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is the tripartite standard on unpaid caregiving leave but it is voluntary, only covers hospitalisation events and has only been adopted by a relatively small fraction of employers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also encourages employees to first use their paid annual leave.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, we are back to the same challenge which I raised in my maiden speech – caregivers burning annual leave time meant for their own rest with no income protection.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans should not have to choose between caring for their loved ones and taking care of themselves.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I call on MSF to seriously consider these recommendations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This raises questions about regional efforts to curb child trafficking.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Domestically, he highlighted that child trafficking was criminalised under the Adoption of Children Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He further stressed the robustness of the adoption process, which included the verification of the child's identity papers, travel documents and conducting checks with birth parents to ensure they had given valid consent and had not offered the child for adoption for improper financial or material gain.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In 2022, MSF tabled the Adoption of Children Bill to introduce a specific regulatory framework governing adoption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The framework includes a requirement for adoptive parents to disclose to the Court the payments they have made to the birth parents and others in the process, and to seek the Court sanctions for these payments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It would also be an offence to obtain the birth parents' consent by fraud, duress or undue influence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The question is, when it comes to children's source from overseas, how effective are these provisions?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In the meantime, adoptive parents would have to pay higher childcare-related expenses without a clear endpoint, which has been straining and demoralising.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to state that I am a foster parent registered with MSF.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But there are about 600 plus foster parents.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think we should put more effort into generating awareness among the communities, working with the fostering agency, such as Boys' Towns, Gracehaven, Muhammadiyah Association and PPIS Home for Good.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The other thing is the foster parents; that they are "on" 24/7.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: They cannot access the school portal and they cannot book online medical.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Those are the issues that the Ministry might want to consider doing a design-thinking project.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Go through the full journey for the foster parents and the foster kids, and see where are the pain points.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Give them the full access since the kids are the primary persons whom we are looking after.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The other thing is a much more holistic way of looking at fostering.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I think currently is the trial systems, where you have the biological parents, the foster parents.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: They do not really talk to each other and then you have the case workers serving as "in-betweens".

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It has its positive and there is the reason for it being so – so they do not sort of interact too much or have conflicts with each other.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: However, I think we can explore much more intensive co-parenting, in situations that are possible, to bring both foster parents and the biological parents together, with the kids as the centre of our attention.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The whole idea for us as foster parents, is to stabilise the kid, gain trust, build bonds and then interact or integrate them back with the biological parents.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: That is our mission and we want to make sure that the bonds continue, rather than disrupted halfway.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, I rise to speak on divorcing couples.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But let me start with a quick clarification.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But I am speaking about divorce today because in Singapore has been going on an upward trend.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In particular, I wish to address the support that MSF provides to help parents transition from being spouses to being co-parents.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Divorce is not merely the end of a marriage.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For many families, it is the beginning of a long co-parenting journey and the people who pay the highest price when that journey is poorly managed are the children.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The online e-learning component to set a baseline understanding, followed by a physical counselling session to discuss practical co-parenting arrangements after divorce is good.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It rightly treats co-parenting as a public good.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But if we accept that, then the support must be timely, accessible and directed to the parents who need it most.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I urge MSF to strengthen delivery of the programme in three ways.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, increase counsellor capacity and appointment slots, including weekends and weekdays.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, expand the schemes to more locations, which includes increasing Family Service Centre capacity where demand is persistently high.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Third, use video sessions in suitable cases so physical capacity constraints do not become a bottleneck.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Next, Chairman, if the programme's purpose is to protect children by improving co-parenting readiness, there appears to be a gap in who is required to attend.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If such a parent is outside the programme, the intervention reaches only one side of the co-parenting, which undermines the policy purpose.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I therefore urge MSF to consider applying the programme more equally to all parents undergoing divorce with children under 21 years old.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, this connects to a second issue that often arises in higher-conflict divorces and it is one that is particularly acute during festive periods when children's access and family time become more emotionally charged.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: During this Lunar New Year period, many families are reuniting and celebrating, but for some parents it is the toughest time of the year because their child has been unilaterally taken away or withheld by the other parent without any Court Order, contact is cut off and they are simply told to "go to Court".

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The cruelty is that legal processes take time and in these cases time matters most, because the first days and weeks of separation can disrupt the child's routines, allow untrue narratives to take hold and erode the child's bond with the left-behind parent.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In other words: justice delayed is justice denied.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, I ask MSF: what more can be done, together with the wider family justice system, to ensure that children are not left to bear the consequences of time delays in high-conflict cases where contact is abruptly cut off?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, these are practical refinements to existing problems, but they go to the heart of what MSF stands for.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Strong families are not only built before a crisis, they are also protected through a crisis.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I hope the Ministry will consider these improvements so that the system achieves what it is meant to achieve: better co-parenting, less conflict and better outcomes for children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, the misuse of AI, particularly through sexually exploitative deepfake content, is creating new risks.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Children and vulnerable persons, including persons with disabilities, may face impersonation, coercion and greater difficulty reporting harm.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How is MSF working with other Government agencies to strengthen digital literacy among parents and caregivers?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there specialised support services for victims of AI-enabled exploitation, particularly children and persons with disabilities?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the call to build a "we first" society reminds us that growth must uplift every family and that care cannot be left to individuals alone.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They shoulder responsibilities not just for themselves, but for their families and loved ones, often while continuing to work and contribute to society.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For many caregivers, the challenge is not only financial support, but having the confidence that help will be there in a timely and predictable way, as care needs evolve unpredictably over time.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: With that, it also brings us as a "we first" society.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We must also care for those who serve others.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Social service professionals and MSF officers operate in a high-touch, emotionally demanding environment, often under manpower constraints.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: As the Ministry advances digitalisation and service transformation, how is it ensuring caseload sustainability, safeguarding officers' career development and upskilling, mental wellbeing and mitigating risks of burnout, so that the social services sector remains a rewarding and sustainable career for officers?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: If we truly believe in "we first", then caregivers and the officers who walk alongside them, must feel that the system stands firmly with them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, some lower-income families face layered and persistent challenges that cannot be resolved quickly even with well designed incentives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: They may be coping with unstable employment, caregiving responsibilities, debt, housing constraints, or children with additional developmental needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: These challenges often interact and compound one another, even when families are making sincere efforts, attending coaching, enrolling in programmes, seeking employment or upgrading skills.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Milestones, such as clearing debt, sustaining employment, or ensuring consistent preschool attendance take time, especially when setbacks occur.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In such circumstances, achievement-based progress package, though well intention may feel distant and difficult to attain.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: When goals seem too ambitious, families may feel discouraged despite genuine effort.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Recognising incremental progress and celebrating step by step gains will better support families on a realistic and dignified path towards stability and upward mobility.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How does MSF plan to strengthen the Comlink+ ecosystem, including both employers and community partners, to better recruit, support and retain beneficiaries in sustained employment?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My both cuts will address guardrails for protecting our children in low-income families.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the book "Alone together", author Turkle examines the increasing reliance on digital devices and social media and the paradox of being alone, together.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Feeling both connected and disconnected in an increasingly digital world.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Apart from loneliness, academic studies show how technology addition leads to anxiety, depression and even aggression and attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder symptoms.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my house visits to rental blocks, I often see parents occupying children and even infants, with screens – smartphones, tablets and TVs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Parents have shared with me their challenges of being busy at work, health or caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, children are often left to their own devices – literally.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this case, the ones occupied with digital screens are unsupervised and without parental restriction guardrails.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is crucial that whilst we push nationwide for a reduction of our children's exposure to screens in schools and age appropriate content, our home environments are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my interactions with families, I have observed recurring challengea: families who remain uncooperative or deeply disengaged.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is often driven by the exhaustion of juggling multiple commitments, personal crisis or a lack of trust in the cobbling system.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This lack of engagement creates a critical blind spot.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It makes it difficult for family coaches to assess genuine needs, maintain continuity of care, or escalate cases where serious concerns, such as family violence or child safety may be involved.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When engagement is inconsistent, the human touch and the trust built by a dedicated coach are easily lost.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must recognise that unresponsiveness itself is often a signal of deeper and more complex challenges.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We cannot allow these families, especially their children, to fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, would the Ministry consider a formal escalation pathway for such cases to Family Service Centres for deeper social work intervention when initial coaching efforts fail to gain traction?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ensuring the safety and well-being of the children in these households must remain our absolute priority.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Earlier this term, I spoke of the need for joined-up longitudinal pathways in education, health and careers that follow a family across life's transitions, so that no one is left to fall through the cracks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Budget 2026 takes a meaningful step in this direction through the enhanced ComLink+ framework.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But if ComLink+ is to become the architecture of modern social mobility, five shifts matter.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, integration must be structural, not best effort.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A family may juggle a family coach, a healthcare team, an employment officer and a school representative.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Could we move towards one shared progression plan across agencies – one dashboard, one set of goals, one coordinated journey?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I ask the Minister if MSF is moving in this direction, so families experience genuine integrated support rather than parallel case files?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A small shock can reverse months of work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One trusted person who knows their story, who checks in, who believes in them when they do not believe in themselves can make all the difference.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we scale, how do we protect that relational core as numbers grow?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fourth, measure transformation, not transactions – not just payouts issued, but job retained, sustained preschool attendance, debt reduced, stress stabilised.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Do coaches have the capacity and tools to anchor this deeper work?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With AI reshaping our economy, digital literacy, AI familiarity and tech-enabled income pathways must be part of progression goals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we do not equip families for the economy of tomorrow, we risk stabilising them for yesterday.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we get this right, ComLink+ do more than support families in difficulty.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And in a society facing inequality and technological disruption, belief may be our most precious asset.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us design ComLink+ not only as a ladder out of hardship, but as a national statement that in Singapore, mobility is never accidental.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Government for appointing the Taskforce on Assurance for Families with Persons with Disabilities (PwDs), chaired by Minister of State Goh Pei Ming.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore already has a strong national roadmap in the Enabling Masterplan 2030.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But there are pressing key concerns of families, particularly about adult life after school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The task force cannot give assurance to these families without addressing these key concerns.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We therefore need funding reforms based on a lifespan approach.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us start with the obvious Day Activity Centres (DAC) and residential home models for adults with moderate to high support needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This base amount should be calculated using a realistic norm cost of care, reflecting staffing ratios, programme costs and operational realities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Service providers, such as the social service agencies, are not naive.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If every additional client requires more fundraising, the system becomes unsustainable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Eventually, service providers will withdraw and the Government may have to operate these services directly, which could cost even more.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Funding reform must therefore align care complexity, workforce reality and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Gap two, disability employment resilience in an AI economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If we do nothing, then inclusive hire gains that have been made in our last decade will reverse.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We must therefore shift from protecting old jobs to designing new work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Failure to do so intentionally and effectively risks reversing the years of good work that SG Enable, disability partners and inclusive employers had already put in.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The most common question families ask is this – what happens when parents lose capacity or die?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We therefore should institutionalise life planning and continuity protocols and encourage families to be part of the solution instead of worrying.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When death or incapacity occurs, the system must respond with speed, coordination and stability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Just as ComLink+ supports vulnerable families with a dedicated guide across life transitions, a life navigator could help disability families plan school-to-work transitions, housing options, caregiver ageing and long-term care arrangements.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A resilient system empowers and supports families to act early instead of relying solely on the Government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, on a thoughtful convergence with mainstream elderly services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The line between disability services and elder care services will blur.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many adults with disabilities face similar challenges as seniors in varying degrees, but at a younger age.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore has built strong community infrastructure for ageing – Active Ageing Centres, Community Care Apartments, home- and community-based care services, even Silver Generation Ambassadors and Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If we design a support architecture that connects disability and ageing systems more intelligently and thoughtfully, we reduce duplication, improve outreach and enhance social compact.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is the assurance that families are asking for and the post-school cliff we must level.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wish the task force all its very best.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Twenty-one years ago, I was blessed with my youngest child.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Being his mom has been a joy, but it is also the biggest challenge in my life.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: In the short time I have been a Nominated Member of Parliament, I have had the opportunity to learn more about the Ministry's plans to support families navigating the complex journey of raising and caring for loved ones with special needs.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I am grateful for the assurances that this is an area of priority and a key aspect of our plan to become a more inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: I know that the Government's heart is in the right place, but the key in ensuring that we actually deliver on the stated mission of becoming a more inclusive society is in how we execute our plans.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: For this, we must listen to the families we seek to serve.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Which is why I am going to share my perspective as a parent and a caregiver.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: One, we must provide a stable and secure care environment.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: If you care for someone with special needs, you will know how long it can take to get them acclimatised to a new environment.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This is why the transition periods are the hardest.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: All we want is for them to adjust to a school, vocational institute or DAC that can support their needs as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Upheaval and change is especially traumatic for this vulnerable group.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The shortage of places for those graduating from special education (SPED) has been a problem for years.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) child who has adjusted to the routine of school graduates only to find that there is no ready place for him or her to go to.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Those who graduate from SPED schools should have ready and available placement options for them to ensure a seamless transition.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: For this to happen, we need a lot more funding to DAC providers who have to meet the high costs of delivering such services so that they are able to confidently expand their offerings, recruit more trained staff and maintain high-quality care.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Two, we must make such care affordable to those who need it.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The high cost of DAC fees may be resulting in under-representation of the actual demand.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: There is nothing more painful or emasculating to a parent than knowing that they cannot afford to get their child more help or they have to sacrifice the needs of their other children to meet the expenses of the special needs child.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Three, we need to give parents the peace of mind that there is a long-term plan for the continued learning and enhanced meaningful engagement of their special needs adult children.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The biggest fear of parents is, who is going to look after my child when I am gone?

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We need to support the entire family unit, including siblings and extended family members so that they feel ready to shoulder the responsibility of continuing care.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: In this respect, I support Ms Denise Phua's suggestions.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The true measure of our society is in how we treat our most vulnerable and those who care for them.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We must commit to a future where no family is left to struggle in the shadows of a waitlist.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: By providing prompt, guaranteed access to vital services, we are not just helping individual families, we strengthen the very fabric of our community.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interests in this area as the past president of Rainbow Centre Singapore, a social service agency serving persons with disabilities, and as a researcher examining the life course of persons with neurodevelopmental disabilities.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: In a study I conducted about two decades ago, examining the futures of persons with autism in Singapore, what must have been the most difficult question I asked parents was – and that was raised just earlier – what are the plans for your child when you are no longer able to care for him or her?

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Some parents described plans, often involving siblings or relatives.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: For others, the response was silence and many conversations were accompanied by tears.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: In a related work, parents of persons with disabilities consistently ranked outcomes linked to safety, stability and personal satisfaction as their top priorities for their child.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Yet many remained uncertain about how those outcomes will be attained.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: There is now greater urgency for three reasons.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Second, while caregivers are living longer, the gap between lifespan and healthspan means that many parents anticipate a period where they may still be alive, yet no longer physically or cognitively able to provide the sustained care.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Second, while caregivers are living longer, the gap between lifespan and health span means that many parents anticipate a period where they may still be alive, yet no longer physically or cognitively able to provide the sustained care.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: This means fewer siblings and extended kin available to assume long-term caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Taken together, these trends suggest that families of PwDs can no longer, as in the past, rely primarily on informal family support.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Adult disability support often extends across several decades.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: So, this raises for us a broader systems consideration.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Do we have a consistent anticipatory framework for planning the continuity of care and participation of PwDs?

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, I would be grateful if the Minister could clarify the issues raised also earlier by my hon colleagues Ms Denise Phua and Ms Kuah Boon Theng.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: First, whether structured family care pathways are initiated well before caregivers are unable to provide support?

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Second, on how siblings and other potential caregivers are systematically engaged in transition planning.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: And third, how the voices of PwDs themselves are meaningfully incorporated into decisions about their future arrangements, support structures and participation in community life?

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: It is an assurance that our citizens with disabilities will continue to live lives of dignity, stability and participation even when parental care is no longer available.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Chairman, many PwDs and employers remain unaware of available support for inclusive employment and daily living.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: While portals, such as the SG Enabling Guide, provides useful resources, information is spread across multiple platforms, making it difficult for PwDs and caregivers to navigate support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Will the Government consider a single, centralised portal that brings together training, employment, housing, social activities and financial assistance, so PwDs and caregivers can more easily access support?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Chairman, I thank the MSF, especially SG Enable, for the good work in uplifting our PwDs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The Taskforce on Assurance for Families with Persons with Disabilities will also be doing more in three key areas: employment, community living and affordability.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I have families in Jalan Kayu with special needs children.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Key concerns of these families include the availability of education and support services; financial support; whether they can help their children find employment or remain engaged; and what will happen to their children when they pass on.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In one particular case, I met a pair of aged parents last year caring for their 30 plus-year-old autistic son.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: He is on the severe spectrum side of the needs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Since then, the father has passed on and the mother now cares for the son alone.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: What more can be done to improve their employment prospects, or remain engaged and cared for during their lifetime?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: One deaf individual received counselling only after a long search.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MSF aims to foster a Singapore society where all families are supported at every stage of their life to thrive on their terms.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Before I elaborate on our approach, let me outline what my colleagues will share.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Minister of State Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim will detail enhancements to support lower-income families, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua will elaborate on our efforts for families with PwDs and Minister of State Goh Pei Ming will touch on how we will strengthen support for families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At MSF, our policies are anchored on four core principles: family centricity, proactive and upstream intervention, strength-based approached and whole-of-society partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These principles are enduring, even as we face increasingly complex issues.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First, we prioritise family centricity because the family is the basic unit of our society that provides emotional support and imparts values.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Working with individuals may address immediate symptoms, but it does not tackle issues at its roots.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must build strong family relationship in order to bring about sustainable change.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is why, for all children, we seek to set good foundations for optimal health and development within family relationships and environments.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For ComLink+ families, we develop a holistic action plan with the family after assessing their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For PwDs, we do not neglect the well-being of caregivers and family members.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our second principle is proactive and upstream intervention.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We strive to provide early support to build strong foundations and address root causes before they escalate.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Third, we focus on the strength of our clients rather than their deficits.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: By harnessing their strengths and assets, individuals and families are and can be empowered to achieve good outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Fourth, we work with the whole-of-society to weave a strong ecosystem of support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MSF has been working alongside our social service agencies (SSAs), corporates, institutes of higher learnings (IHLs) and the community to better understand clients' needs, finetune our policies and programmes and to journey with our clients.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: When we work together, we unlock new synergies, spark innovation and build better solutions for our clients.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To build a better tomorrow for all families, we will further strengthen these partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will do this through the following "3Cs": collaborating with our partners, cooperating with regional and international counterparts in shared priority areas and co-creating to develop innovations of tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The first "C" refers to working collaboratively with partners to better serve families and individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In recent years, we have stepped up collaboration with sector partners to make a greater impact.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will continue to invest in such collaborations and especially with four key groups: Government agencies, SSAs, corporates and IHLs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First, we are collaborating with Government agencies to better support lower-income families and improve social mobility, a key concern raised by Mr Xie Yao Quan.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Under this model, family coaches and healthcare staff came together to support families to adopt healthy lifestyles and to access suitable services.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Later this year, we will bring more ComLink+ families on board this trial.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With this, more ComLink+ residents can benefit from personalised care from a trusted family doctor, subsidies for screening tests as well as vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They will also be able to access Health Promotion Board programmes via the Healthy 365 app.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will share more details in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Second, we are collaborating with SSAs to support families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, MSF works closely with SSAs under the Strengthening Family Programme, which provides counselling support for them.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over the past decade, we have worked closely with the Family Justice Court to adopt a therapeutic justice model in resolving familial disputes so that the family can benefit from a restorative, holistic and forward-looking approach.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have expanded our support for couples going through divorce, which Ms Diana Pang spoke about.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We hope this will prevent disagreements later over child access.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But if such disagreements arise, couples can still approach the Family Justice Court for mediation or apply for a child access order or to enforce an access order.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We want to encourage more couples to seek help early and not only at the point of divorce.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, MSF will work with Strengthening Family Programme centres to ramp up family counselling capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Members of the public will be able to access both in-person and online counselling services.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In the meantime, we will make and continue to make family counselling more accessible and provide self-help resources online to better support families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Third, we are collaborating with corporates for more impactful philanthropy.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am heartened that many corporates have adopted this framework.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: DBS has also embedded giving into their corporate culture and we hope more organisations will do the same.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Fourth, we are collaborating on research and programme evaluation to build a strong evidence base for tomorrow's solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We work with various IHLs to build up our knowledge base of what works best in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Other partnerships include evaluating effectiveness of ComLink+ Progress Packages with IPS and the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Through these collaborations, we hope that our IHLs will build renowned experts and an impactful body of knowledge on support for families and thereby lead in this field.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The second "C" stands for cooperate; and in this context, cooperating with regional and international partners.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Because we need to work together with others, beyond our shores, in strengthening families, early childhood development and social mobility.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We seek to do this at Government, academia as well as practitioner levels.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is because challenges confronting Singapore are not unique.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: By cooperating with like-minded partners, we can exchange ideas and evolve best practices to better serve our respective clients.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One initiative involves our regional neighbours: Cambodia, the Philippines and Thailand.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They have been keen to learn from our experience in setting up the ECDA and the KidSTART programme.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This programme will establish strong networks and foster cross-sharing of evidence-based approaches to benefit young children and families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Other platforms include conferences where researchers and policy-makers can interact and germinate ideas and relationships.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Last year, MSF and IPS co-organised the inaugural International Conference on Societies of Opportunity (ICSO), bringing together local and international thought leaders to discuss how we can better create opportunities and strengthen social mobility for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will further such collaborations at ICSO in 2027.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We also organised the biennial Asian Family Conference, a dedicated regional policy-practice-research platform to discuss emerging family trends, policies and practices.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Later this year, we will share findings of the inaugural regional collaboration between Singapore and ASEAN member states that will enable us and our regional partners to better support families in our respective countries.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am excited by the new opportunities that such partnerships bring, so that we can do better by and for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Before I go to the third "C", let me touch on our professionals.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To enable them to deliver their best, we must first ensure that they are well-supported and cared for.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari asked about support for professionals' development and well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: SSAs can leverage training subsidies and sponsorships under the Professional Capability Grant to support staff development and upskilling.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Recently, we enhanced the schemes to benefit more professionals to support their development and retention.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For protection practitioners, we launched the Protection Practitioners Care Fund to enable SSAs to implement well-being initiatives and practices to support them even better.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Officers at MSF can access Well-being@Gov, which provides well-being resources, coaching and counselling services. hose in the Protective Services receive additional support including clinical supervision and peer support groups.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But support for our professionals does not stop here.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will leverage AI and technology tools to enhance their quality of life while making work more impactful.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is how the third "C" comes in – co-creation.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Co-creating innovations of tomorrow that will improve the quality of life for social sector professionals and clients.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As the sector developer, NCSS is working closely with public and private sector agencies to develop and drive the adoption of AI and technology solutions across the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One such example is Scribe, a tool developed by Open Government Products that translates and summarises conversations in multiple languages and transforms transcripts into structured notes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Just over the past year, over 100 SSAs have adopted Scribe.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have heard from many social workers that Scribe has saved a lot of time and allowed them to focus on what they care about most – their clients.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For the early childhood sector, Mr Melvin Yong will be pleased to know that under the refreshed Industry Digital Plan, ECDA will be supporting preschools to adopt AI-enabled tools, including AI video analytics solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ultimately, our goal is to ease our professionals' workload, enhance their well-being and improve care and education of our children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At MSF, we have also similarly incorporated AI and technology solutions to support our officers in their work.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, in our Youth Homes, time-consuming processes such as filling out paperwork and cross-referencing files are now digitalised under the Home Central Information System.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Officers also use AI tools such as Pair and AIBots that generate first drafts to help officers work more efficiently.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Taken together, Youth Guidance Officers such as Mr Rayner Hoe, now have more bandwidth to engage with youths, which is the most fulfilling part of the job.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Beyond these examples, there is still much more potential for technology to be harnessed to improve the quality of life for our professionals.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But I will now turn to our clients.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In the past few years, MSF has worked closely with the sector to co-create innovative solutions to make our services more client-centric.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
